findings.title: Array index taken from a query string sizes an unbounded slice allocation in deepObject decoding
findings.impact: An unauthenticated remote client crashes the server process with a single short request: Go's out-of-memory condition is a fatal runtime error that net/http's per-connection recover cannot catch, so this is process termination and not merely a dropped connection. The index costs the attacker ten bytes and costs the server gigabytes, and the request can be repeated concurrently.
findings.evidence: sliceMapToSlice (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:936-962) parses every map key as an integer with strconv.Atoi (:941), takes the maximum (:947-952) and then grows a slice one element at a time from 0 to that maximum (:953-960). The keys are the bracketed segments of a query-parameter name: urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject's deepObject branch (:661-681) extracts them with the `\[(.*?)\]` capture at :669 and joins them into props; makeObject (:911) turns them into nested maps with deepSet (:899-909); buildResObj's array branch (:965-993) hands that map to sliceMapToSlice and then allocates a second slice of the same length with make([]any, len(arr)) at :986. Nothing between the socket and :953 compares the index against a bound. findings.title: Request body is buffered twice in memory when a security requirement is validated
findings.impact: A constant-factor increase in the memory a request costs the server, on top of an unbounded read that the consumer is expected to cap. It gives an attacker nothing they did not already have from sending a large body.
findings.evidence: validateSecurityRequirement reads the whole request body into `data` with io.ReadAll at openapi3filter/validate_request.go:448, then restores req.Body from a closure that captures that same slice (:485-488). ValidateRequest then calls ValidateRequestBody, which reads the body again into a second slice at :271 and installs a second capturing closure at :288-290. Both slices are reachable while the second read is in flight, so peak resident size for the body is twice its length. Neither call site bounds the read: there is no MaxBytesReader, no ContentLength check and no configurable maximum anywhere in openapi3filter/options.go.

findings.title: ZipFileBodyDecoder appends the whole read buffer regardless of bytes read, and decompresses without a bound
findings.impact: Any consumer that registers this decoder validates a body that differs from what was uploaded: bytes the client never sent are appended, and content from one archive entry bleeds into the decoded value of another within the same request. A schema check performed on that value is a check on the wrong bytes, so it can both reject valid input and accept input the archive did not contain.
findings.evidence: The read loop at openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1636-1647 does `n, err := rc.Read(buffer)` and then, on `if 0 < n`, `content = append(content, buffer...)` at :1639 - the whole 256-byte buffer rather than buffer[:n]. Every short read therefore contributes 256 bytes to the decoded value: trailing zero bytes on the first pass and, on later passes, the residue of whatever was read before, including bytes from the previous entry of the same archive. The decoded string handed to schema validation is consequently not the archive's content. In the same function the capacity at :1623 is `make([]byte, 0, bufferSize*len(zr.File))`, sized from the entry count declared in the uploaded archive, and the loop from :1626 concatenates every entry with no ceiling on the total; the doc comment at :1608-1609 acknowledges this second half ('Use with caution as this implementation may be susceptible to a z

findings.title: Nil regular-expression matcher is dereferenced when a schema pattern fails to compile and MultiError is enabled
findings.impact: Every request carrying a string value for the affected property panics inside request validation. Under net/http the connection is reset with no response and a stack trace is logged; outside a recovered handler goroutine the process terminates. The panic is triggered by ordinary traffic, so it is a permanent outage of that operation rather than an attacker-timed event.
findings.evidence: visitJSONString's pattern block (openapi3/schema.go:2654-2669) loads a cached matcher, and on a miss calls compilePattern at :2659. When compilation fails and settings.multiError is set, the error is appended to the accumulator at :2662 and execution continues to `if !cp.MatchString(value)` at :2666. cp is not usable at that point: compilePattern (openapi3/schema_pattern.go:16-32) assigns the result of regexp.Compile into the named return `cp RegexMatcher` at :21, so on failure cp holds a typed nil *regexp.Regexp - a non-nil interface whose method call dereferences a nil receiver - and the error arm returns at :31 without clearing it. With a custom RegexCompilerFunc (:19) the same line yields whatever the compiler returned, commonly an untyped nil interface, which also panics on the call. The non-MultiError path is unaffected because :2661 returns first.

findings.title: External $ref resolution reads any local path and any HTTP URL with no allowlist hook short of replacing the reader
findings.impact: A consumer that loads documents it did not write - an API gateway ingesting a customer-supplied spec, a linting service, a CI job validating an untrusted file - and enables external refs gives the document author a read primitive over the process's filesystem (`$ref: "/etc/passwd"`) and an outbound request from the server's network position (`$ref: "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"`), with the fetched bytes surfaced through the parsed document or through the parse error.
findings.evidence: DefaultReadFromURI (openapi3/loader_uri_reader.go:46) chains ReadFromHTTP(http.DefaultClient) and ReadFromFile. ReadFromHTTP (:51-70) issues a GET to whatever URL the document names, with the default client - which follows up to ten redirects - and no scheme, host, port or address check; ReadFromFile (:79-84) calls os.ReadFile on path.Clean of the document's path with no base-directory containment. The gate is the single boolean IsExternalRefsAllowed, checked at openapi3/loader.go:118-120 and :348-350, with the test itself at :107-112, and it is all-or-nothing: there is no hook to allow one host or one directory. It is also skipped entirely when a custom ReadFromURIFunc is installed (openapi3/loader.go:118 and :348), which the field's own comment documents as a security-relevant delegation (openapi3/loader.go:39-48). findings.title: OpenAPI 3.1 validation fails open to a validator that ignores every 2020-12 keyword
findings.impact: Constraints the document author wrote are silently not enforced. An input that an `if/then/else` branch, a `dependentRequired` rule, a `patternProperties` restriction or a `contains` bound was meant to reject is accepted by the validator, and the application behind it receives data it believes was checked. The failure is silent by construction: no error, no log line, no difference visible to the caller.
findings.evidence: useJSONSchema2020 (openapi3/schema_jsonschema_validator.go:204-212) discards the constructor's error - `if err != nil { return schema.visitJSON(settings, value) }` at :206-209, with the comment 'Fall back to built-in validator if compilation fails'. Nothing is logged and nothing is returned to the caller, so a document whose 2020-12 schema will not compile is validated by the built-in engine and reports success. The built-in engine implements none of the 2020-12 keywords: visitJSON (openapi3/schema.go:1951-2048) handles not, oneOf, anyOf, allOf, enum and const before dispatching by type; visitJSONObject (:2831-2993) handles properties, minProperties, maxProperties, additionalProperties and required; visitJSONArray (:2732-2823) handles minItems, maxItems, uniqueItems and items. The fields If, Then, Else, DependentRequired, DependentSchemas, PatternProperties, PropertyNames, PrefixItems, C

findings.title: Schema validation errors embed the failing value and the full schema by default
findings.impact: A consumer that returns the validation error to the caller - which ConvertErrors and ValidationErrorEncoder exist to make easy - echoes the rejected value back, and with it the internal schema, including property names, formats, patterns and bounds that were not otherwise published. The rejected value is frequently the sensitive one: a password that failed a pattern, a token that failed a format.
findings.evidence: SchemaError.Error (openapi3/schema.go:3086-3132) ends with `if !SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled` at :3120 and then JSON-encodes both the schema (:3124) and the offending value (:3128) into the message. SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled is declared false at openapi3/schema.go:34, so details are on unless the consumer flips a package-level global. The struct's own comment on the Reason field (:3038) states the opposite intent - 'The message should never include the original value to prevent leakage of potentially sensitive inputs in error messages' - which the Value block at :3127-3129 contradicts. The error text is not confined to logs: openapi3filter/validation_error_encoder.go:74-78 puts e.Error() into ValidationError.Title, and openapi3filter/errors.go composes RequestError messages from the wrapped cause.

findings.title: Decoding an array parameter whose schema omits items dereferences a nil SchemaRef
findings.impact: Any request supplying that parameter aborts request handling. Under net/http the connection is reset with no response and a stack trace is logged; outside a recovered handler goroutine the process terminates. Because the trigger is ordinary traffic rather than a crafted value, the affected operation is unusable rather than intermittently attackable.
findings.evidence: parseArray (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1103-1120) passes schemaRef.Value.Items straight to parsePrimitive at :1106, and parsePrimitive's first statement (:1128) is `schema.Value.Type.Slice()`. When the array schema has no `items`, Items is nil and that line dereferences a nil *openapi3.SchemaRef. urlValuesDecoder.parseArray does the same at :555 into parseValue, whose first statement reads schema.Value.AllOf. All four decoders reach it: pathParamDecoder.DecodeArray (:394), urlValuesDecoder.DecodeArray (:522), headerParamDecoder.DecodeArray (:744) and cookieParamDecoder.DecodeArray (:805), each selected by decodeValue at :323 whenever the parameter schema's type is `array`. The document is not rejected first: Schema.validate only requires `items` for arrays when 2020-12 validation is off (openapi3/schema.go:1690, `if schema.Items == nil && !validationOpts.jsonSchema2020ValidationE

findings.title: CI executes third-party actions by mutable tag and Go tools by @latest
findings.impact: Whoever controls one of those upstream repositories, or a tag on them, executes arbitrary code inside the CI job on every push and pull request. The job holds GITHUB_TOKEN in its environment (go.yml:10, see F-005) and its working tree is the repository being built, so a compromised tool can both read the token and modify the source it is asked to format.
findings.evidence: Not one `uses:` in either workflow is pinned by commit SHA: go.yml references actions/setup-go@v6 (:28, :199), actions/cache@v3 (:33), actions/checkout@v6 (:43, :198); shellcheck.yml references actions/checkout@v2 (:12) and ludeeus/action-shellcheck@1.1.0 (:15). That is 0 of 7 `uses:` references pinned, across 5 distinct actions. Three steps go further and resolve third-party Go modules at run time from a floating pointer: `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/modernize/cmd/modernize@latest -test -diff -fix` at go.yml:59, which is invoked with `-fix` and therefore rewrites the checked-out tree; `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/nilness/cmd/nilness@latest` at :99; and `go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest` at :202, whose binary is then run over every Go file at :204. `@latest` and a git tag are both mutable pointers: the code that runs tomorrow nee

findings.title: OpenAPI 3.1 validation recompiles the whole JSON Schema on every request
findings.impact: For an OpenAPI 3.1 document, each request pays a CPU cost proportional to the size of the resolved schema for the parameter or body it targets - a full marshal, unmarshal, recursive rewrite and schema compilation, including recompilation of every `pattern` in that subtree. An unauthenticated client turns a small request into that fixed work, repeatedly and concurrently, which is an amplification factor rather than a constant overhead. It also means the pattern cache the library maintains for the 3.0 path buys nothing on the 3.1 path.
findings.evidence: VisitJSON dispatches to useJSONSchema2020 whenever the caller passed EnableJSONSchema2020 (openapi3/schema.go:1942-1948), and useJSONSchema2020 calls newJSONSchemaValidator(schema) at openapi3/schema_jsonschema_validator.go:205 on every invocation. That constructor marshals the entire schema to JSON (:21), unmarshals it back into a map (:27), walks the whole tree rewriting keywords (:32, recursive at :116/:126/:137), builds a brand-new jsonschema.Compiler (:35) and compiles the resource (:45). Nothing is memoised: the only cache in the package is compiledPatterns (openapi3/schema.go:46), which holds individual `pattern` regexps and is not consulted here, and the constructed validator is discarded when useJSONSchema2020 returns. openapi3filter takes this path for every 3.1 document and on every request: EnableJSONSchema2020 is appended at openapi3filter/validate_request.go:242-244 for eac

findings.title: AWS access key identifier present in a vendored OpenAPI test fixture
findings.impact: None demonstrated. An AWS access key identifier is not by itself a credential - the secret access key is what authenticates - and the accompanying signature is scoped to one object and one hour, both of which elapsed in 2017. The fact is recorded so a future scanner hit on this line is triaged once rather than repeatedly.
findings.evidence: A working-tree scan for the distinctive credential formats named in SUP-16 (GitHub personal, OAuth, user, server and refresh tokens; AWS access key identifiers; Anthropic API keys; Slack tokens; Google API keys; and PEM private-key headers), run over the whole target excluding .git, returned exactly one hit: line 29766 of openapi3/testdata/oai_v3_stoplight.json carries an example S3 pre-signed URL containing `X-Amz-Credential=[REDACTED:secret]` and `X-Amz-Signature=[REDACTED:secret]` alongside `X-Amz-Date=20170728...` and `X-Amz-Expires=3600`. The surrounding document is a vendored third-party API specification kept as a parser fixture; the string is an example value inside it, not configuration this project reads. No hit was found anywhere in non-test Go source for password, secret, token or api-key literals.

findings.title: PathItem.GetOperation panics on any unrecognised HTTP method and the legacy router reaches it with the client's method
findings.impact: An unauthenticated remote client aborts request handling with `curl -X FOO http://host/<a static path from the spec>`. Under net/http the panic is caught by the per-connection recover, so the connection is reset with no response and a full stack trace is written to the server log: repeated at rate this is log amplification and wasted CPU, not process death. Outside a net/http handler goroutine - a framework without panic recovery, or an application that calls FindRoute from a worker, a warm-up or a batch job - the same call terminates the process.
findings.evidence: GetOperation (openapi3/path_item.go:153-175) switches over the nine methods named in net/http and its default arm is `panic(fmt.Errorf("unsupported HTTP method %q", method))` at :174. routers/legacy/router.go:108-153 calls it with the raw request method: FindRoute takes `method := req.Method` (:109), asks the pathpattern tree for a match (:141) and, when no route came back, looks the path up directly and calls `pathItem.GetOperation(method)` at :150. The tree cannot absorb an unknown method: CreateNode registers every route as the literal string `METHOD + " " + path` (routers/legacy/router.go:70) and matchRemaining compares constant prefixes (routers/legacy/pathpattern/node.go:275-281), so `FOO /pets` matches no `GET `/`POST ` prefix, Match returns nil, and control reaches :146. Paths.Value(remainingPath) returns the PathItem for any statically declared path, and :150 then panics. An HTT

findings.title: GitHub Actions workflows declare no permissions block while exposing GITHUB_TOKEN to every step
findings.impact: If the repository default is read-write - the platform default unless changed - then any code that executes inside build-and-test holds a token that can write repository contents, and the workflow deliberately executes third-party code from mutable @latest references. The consequence of a compromised upstream tool is not a failed build but a writable repository.
findings.evidence: Neither .github/workflows/go.yml nor .github/workflows/shellcheck.yml contains a `permissions:` key at workflow or job level, so both inherit whatever default the repository or organization sets for GITHUB_TOKEN. go.yml additionally lifts the token into the job environment at :10 (`GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`), which makes it visible to every step of build-and-test rather than only to the steps that need it - and those steps include third-party code fetched at run time (`go run golang.org/x/tools/.../modernize@latest` at :59, `go run golang.org/x/tools/.../nilness@latest` at :99, `go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest` at :202) and `go generate ./...` at :45. Both workflows trigger on `push` as well as `pull_request` (go.yml:3-4, shellcheck.yml:3-5), so the token in a push run is the repository's own, not a fork's read-only one.

advisories_to_match.summary: kin-openapi has uncontrolled resource consumption in openapi3filter deepObject query parameter decoding
advisories_to_match.description:
### Summary

An uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability in `openapi3filter` lets any unauthenticated client force multi-gigabyte heap allocation with a single, tiny HTTP request. When a spec declares a `deepObject`-style query parameter whose schema contains an array (a normal, documented pattern), the decoder reconstructs the array by reading the **largest attacker-supplied index** and allocating one slot for every position from `0` up to that index — *before* schema validation (including `maxItems`) ever runs. A request as small as 24 bytes (`?param[items][50000000]=x`) drives heap allocation to **~6.1 GiB**, reliably triggering an OOM kill / restart loop on memory-constrained services.

### Details

The OpenAPI `style: deepObject` serialization lets clients express arrays in the query string using bracket notation, e.g. `param[items][0]=a&param[items][1]=b`. The decoder first collects these into an intermediate `map[string]any` keyed by the string of the index, then converts that sparse map into a real `[]any` in [`sliceMapToSlice`](https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/blob/master/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go#L936):

```go
// req_resp_decoder.go (vulnerable versio
